passages.text: Modern vehicles include dozens of safety technologies designed to reduce injuries during collisions, but few systems react as quickly as airbags. Hidden behind steering wheels, dashboards, seats, pillars, and roof panels, airbags remain inactive during normal driving yet become fully inflated within milliseconds during a crash. Most drivers never see airbags deployed in real life, which often creates curiosity about how fast they actually work and what happens during those critical moments after impact. Airbags are designed to work together with seat belts to reduce the force experienced by occupants during sudden collisions. Their speed is extremely important because vehicle crashes happen faster than human reaction time. The airbag system must detect the crash, decide whether deployment is necessary, ignite the inflator, fill the airbag completely, and begin deflating almost instantly before the occupant moves forward significantly. Although airbags save thousands of lives every year, many people misunderstand how they operate, how quickly they deploy, and why deployment force can sometimes cause injuries as well. Understanding how airbags work helps drivers better appreciate modern vehicle safety engineering and understand why proper seating position and seat belt use remain so important.
